The Ants and the Cicada: Does Preparing for the Future Entitle You to Judge Someone Else's Summer?
As autumn drew to a close, the ants were drying the grain they had stored during the summer.
A hungry cicada approached and asked them to share a little food.
The ants asked:
Why didn't you prepare during the summer?
The cicada answered:
I was singing all the time and never got around to storing anything.
So the ants said:
Since you sang in summer, you can dance in winter.

In the later, familiar children's version, the cicada often becomes a grasshopper with a fiddle tucked under its arm. Singing is then more explicitly called “play,” while the ants' food gathering is called “work.” The story ends with a tidy lesson:
There is a time for work and a time for play.
This moral captures an unavoidable fact:
Winter will not supply food automatically because the summer's music was beautiful.
But it also compresses several different questions into one.
Was failing to prepare for the future a mistake?
Does singing have no value?
Does bearing the consequences of one's choices mean others should let one starve?
And does possessing stored food give someone the right to pass judgment on another's entire summer?
These are not the same question.
Let us first acknowledge the story's firmest ground.
Survival requires basic conditions.

Food must at some point be obtained, preserved, or produced anew. Someone may value music, games, travel, research, or any activity that cannot immediately be exchanged for food. These activities do not abolish the body's needs.
If throughout the summer the cicada could see winter coming and had the ability to store food, yet made no preparation at all, then its winter predicament really is connected to its earlier choices.
Placing all the responsibility on the ants would be unfair.

The ants worked during the summer. They gave up some immediate ease to prepare for a problem that could not be solved on the spot in winter. The story has good reason to praise this ability to look ahead.
If life attends only to the present, every change becomes an immediate crisis.

Saving, planning, maintenance, and training all preserve room for later action. Preparation does not mean fearing life. Often, it is precisely because someone took on a burden in advance that the future offers more than forced reactions.
This essay cannot defend the cicada by calling the ants' labor narrow-minded, or pretend that a material foundation is merely some lower-order need.
Without food, music cannot continue either.
The question has never been whether the basic conditions matter.
It is whether their importance also means that every hour not directly producing stored food has no value.
The later fiddle version quietly answers that question for us.
It calls the ants' summer work and the grasshopper's summer play.
Once things are named that way, winter's verdict is almost settled.
The worker has food because the worker is responsible.
The player has none because the player squandered the summer.
But the story never fully explains what “singing” is.
It may be merely the cicada's own amusement.
It may also bring sound and rhythm to the life around it.
It may be instinct, or an ability requiring practice.
None of these possibilities stores food for the cicada, but they do affect how we understand what it did all summer.
If an activity cannot be eaten or directly exchanged for the resources of survival in winter, does it amount only to “not working”?
That judgment is too quick.
Life contains many things that cannot be stored directly as grain: companionship, care, creation, exploration, celebrations, games, and activities that sustain a community's feelings and memories.
They cannot replace basic material conditions.
But a world that recognizes only activities convertible into reserves will end up with many warehouses and increasing difficulty explaining what kind of life those warehouses protect.
The ants preserve food to survive the winter.
And after surviving it?
If the answer is only to keep storing food for the next winter, the means may gradually take over the end.
That does not make food storage wrong.
It simply reminds us that what sustains life and what makes life worth continuing may not be entirely the same.
Next comes a harder question:
Should the ants share food with the cicada?
The fable gives us too few facts to answer easily.
We do not know how much food the ants have.
We do not know how long the winter will be.
We do not know whether sharing a little would endanger the entire colony.
We do not know whether the cicada has another way to obtain food.
Nor do we know whether it has previously helped sustain their shared life.
Without this information, immediately condemning the ants as cruel is no more careful than immediately condemning the cicada as lazy.
If the stores are barely enough for the colony to survive, demanding that the ants prove their kindness by dying themselves is plainly unreasonable.
If food is abundant and the cicada faces imminent death, whether “This was your own choice” dissolves every duty to help deserves further questioning.
Being responsible for one's predicament does not give every onlooker a justifiable reason to let it reach its worst possible outcome.
Responsibility and assistance are not alternatives from which we may choose only one.
We can say:
You need to face the consequences of failing to prepare.
And also say:
That does not mean hunger itself is a punishment you deserve.
Help can also come with reasonable conditions.

We can first provide the minimum needed to sustain life, then discuss together how to prepare next time. We can ask the recipient to contribute to work they can undertake later. We can also make resource limits clear, so that one act of aid does not become a permanent claim on someone else's labor.
All these approaches draw distinctions missing from “Since you missed your summer, you should starve in winter.”
Fables favor direct consequences because they make the lesson clearest.
The cicada stores no food, so it is hungry in winter.
The ants store food, so they are safe in winter.
But resources in the real world are rarely distributed so neatly.
Some people work extremely hard and still have inadequate reserves.
Some possess reserves not only through their own diligence, but through their starting point, circumstances, cooperation, and luck.
Some spent the summer doing enormous amounts of work that could not be stored as personal wealth but sustained other people's lives.
Others never had the information, time, or resources needed to prepare for winter.
A fable can set these conditions aside to bring “preparation” into focus.
Readers cannot directly extend the conclusion of that simplified setting into a judgment on everyone who lacks resources.
When we see someone asking for food in winter, it is easy to imagine they spent the whole summer choosing irresponsibility.
But “They have none now” tells us only what they currently lack. It cannot reconstruct, by itself, the choices they once had.
If we turn an outcome into a judgment of character without understanding those conditions, we mistake the fable's simplification for the whole of reality.
It would be equally dishonest to invent a noble backstory for the cicada.
We cannot oppose an ethic of diligence by announcing that its song must have served everyone, or that the ants enjoyed music all summer and therefore owe it food.
The text does not say that.
The cicada may really have thought only of the moment.
It may have misjudged the season, underestimated the future, or assumed someone would always help when the time came.
It still needs to face these things.
Calling a choice “art” or “freedom” does not stop it from having real consequences.
Even something truly one's own needs conditions in the body, in time, and in shared life that allow it to continue.
If every shortfall in the basics demands unconditional support from others, that direction has not yet fully taken responsibility for its own existence.
This essay therefore does not side with the cicada against the ants.
It preserves the facts on each side that the other cannot cancel:
The cicada cannot use song to deny food.
The ants cannot use food to deny song.
“Preparing for the future” is an important ability.
But it easily turns from an ability into a moral ranking.
The better someone is at accumulating reserves, the more readily they may believe they are not merely safer, but more entitled to say how others should live.
Savings become evidence of self-discipline.
A lack of savings becomes evidence of frivolity.
Producing measurable results becomes contribution.
Activities that cannot be directly priced become consumption.
Sometimes this judgment identifies real responsibility. Sometimes it squeezes complex lives into a single measure.
The ants can say:
I prepared for my winter, so I should not be required to surrender everything I need to sustain myself.
But they cannot take that statement alone and conclude:
Therefore your summer had no value, and your hunger proves that you are a lesser being than I am.
Better preparation shows only that someone did better at this particular ability.
It does not automatically complete an assessment of another life.
The cicada, too, faces an uncomfortable question.
If it truly values singing, is it willing to learn how to keep singing through the winter?

That may mean setting aside some summer time to prepare food, finding cooperation, or adjusting its way of life. Not to make music a money-making tool, but to keep music from existing only on condition that others provide its material foundation.
Protecting a value that is not instrumental does not mean refusing to establish a practical foundation for it.
Precisely because it matters, it needs to be able to last.
Seen this way, the ants' ability need not merely oppose the cicada's.
The cicada may need to learn part of it: not to turn every hour into stored grain, but to preserve a winter for the life it truly values.
Conversely, the ants may need the cicada's reminder that storing food is not the only thing worth becoming good at in a lifetime.
This is not a warm rewriting in which both sides learn from each other.
The original story offers no such reconciliation.
It shows only that once a survival crisis has arrived, many questions that could have been discussed in summer shrink into the cruel choice of whether to share food.
What the fable can actually demonstrate, then, is a narrower judgment:
Making no preparation when we know future needs will arise imposes costs on our future selves and on others.
It cannot establish, on its own:
That every activity without a stored result is merely play.
That the well-prepared are therefore worth more.
That the underprepared should suffer the worst possible consequences.
That a resource-holder's refusal needs no further scrutiny.
Summer and winter really are different.
Some things must be done while there is still time.
But we prepare for winter not to make winter the only season.
Food lets life continue.
Song may keep that continuing life from being only an exercise in self-preservation.
Neither can replace the other, and neither should cancel the other.
The truly difficult question has never been whether work or singing matters more.
It is:
How can we build a foundation sufficient to sustain life without giving the way we build it authority to judge everything life contains?

*Textual basis: Aesopic tradition, Perry Index 373, whose title in early indexing is usually “The Cicada and the Ants.” The opening follows the later popular version in the 1919 The Æsop for Children, which recasts the characters as a fiddle-playing grasshopper and ants, with the explicit moral “There is a time for work and a time for play.” This essay also examines that work/play division itself, rather than silently projecting it backward as the sole answer of every earlier version.*
